Physiology-2.question: ১) What is the speed of conduction (m/s) for Bundle of His?
Physiology-2.exp:
The Bundle of His conducts electrical impulses at approximately 1 m/s.

High-yield cardiac conduction velocities:

  • SA node: ~0.05 m/s

  • AV node: ~0.05 m/s (slowest conduction)

  • Bundle of His: ~1 m/s

  • Purkinje fibers: ~4 m/s (fastest conduction)

  • Atrial & ventricular muscle: ~0.3–0.5 m/s

The other options correspond to:

  • 0.05 m/s – SA node/AV node

  • 0.5 m/s – Approximate ventricular muscle conduction

  • 4 m/s – Purkinje fibers

Physiology-2.question: ২) The ECG waves are predominantly negative in which of the following?
Physiology-2.exp:
In a normal ECG, lead aVR records electrical activity directed away from the right arm, so the mean cardiac depolarization vector moves away from this lead. As a result:

  • P wave → Negative

  • QRS complex → Predominantly negative

  • T wave → Usually negative

The other leads are usually predominantly positive:

  • aVL – Usually positive or biphasic.

  • aVF – Usually positive.

  • Lead II – Typically has the tallest positive P wave and a predominantly positive QRS complex.

High-yield recall:

  • Predominantly negative lead: aVR

  • Lead with tallest positive P wave: Lead II

  • Fastest conduction: Purkinje fibers (4 m/s)

Physiology-2.question: ৩) Cardiac muscle can’t be fatigued and tetanized due to which of the following characteristic?
Physiology-2.exp:
Cardiac muscle cannot be tetanized because it has a prolonged absolute refractory period, which lasts almost as long as the contraction itself. This prevents summation of contractions and ensures that the heart relaxes between beats to allow ventricular filling.

The prolonged refractory period also contributes to the heart's resistance to fatigue under normal physiological conditions.

The other options are incorrect:

  • Contractility – Ability of the myocardium to contract.

  • Automaticity – Ability to generate spontaneous impulses.

  • Tonicity – Basal muscle tone; not responsible for preventing tetanus.

High-yield recall:

  • Skeletal muscle: Short refractory period → Can be tetanized.

  • Cardiac muscle: Long refractory period (~250 ms) → Cannot be tetanized.

Physiology-2.question: ৪) Which of the following is true about atrial fibrillation?
Physiology-2.exp:
Atrial fibrillation (AF) is characterized by:

  • Absent P waves

  • Irregularly irregular rhythm

  • Presence of fibrillatory (f) waves

  • Variable ventricular response

  • Pulse deficit (apical pulse rate exceeds the peripheral pulse rate because some ventricular contractions do not generate a palpable pulse)

The other options are incorrect:

  • Enlarged P wave – Seen in atrial enlargement, but P waves are absent in AF.

  • Multiple N wave – Not an ECG feature of atrial fibrillation.

  • Tall (peaked/tented) P wave – Seen in right atrial enlargement (P pulmonale), not AF.

High-yield recall:

  • ECG in AF: No P waves + fibrillatory (f) waves + irregularly irregular RR intervals

  • Clinical sign: Pulse deficit

Physiology-2.question: ৫) What is the duration of first rapid inflow during cardiac cycle?
Physiology-2.exp:
The first rapid inflow phase (rapid ventricular filling phase) occurs immediately after the AV valves open at the beginning of ventricular diastole. During this phase, approximately 70–80% of ventricular filling occurs passively.

Duration of phases of the cardiac cycle (at 75 beats/min):

  • Isovolumetric relaxation: ~0.08 sec

  • First rapid inflow (rapid filling): ~0.11 sec (0.113 sec) ✔️

  • Diastasis (slow filling): ~0.19 sec

  • Atrial systole: ~0.10 sec

The other options are incorrect because they do not correspond to the normal duration of the rapid filling phase.

Physiology-2.question: ৬) What is responsible for Plateau in action potential of ventricular muscles?
Physiology-2.exp:
The plateau phase (Phase 2) of the ventricular muscle action potential is mainly due to the opening of slow L-type calcium channels, allowing a prolonged influx of Ca²⁺. At the same time, there is reduced K⁺ efflux, which helps maintain the plateau.

This prolonged depolarization:

  • Produces sustained ventricular contraction.

  • Creates a long refractory period, preventing tetany.

The other options are incorrect:

  • Rapid calcium channel – No such physiologically significant channel in ventricular myocytes.

  • Slow sodium-potassium channel – Does not exist.

  • Fast sodium-potassium channel – Incorrect; rapid Na⁺ channels are responsible for Phase 0 (rapid depolarization).

High-yield recall:

  • Phase 0: Fast Na⁺ channels

  • Phase 1: Transient K⁺ efflux

  • Phase 2 (Plateau): Slow L-type Ca²⁺ channels

  • Phase 3: K⁺ efflux

  • Phase 4: Resting membrane potential

Physiology-2.question: ৭) ECG change in hypokalemia is all except which of the following?
Physiology-2.exp:
The characteristic ECG changes of hypokalemia are:

  • Flattening or inversion of the T wave ✔️

  • ST-segment depression ✔️

  • Prominent U waves ✔️

  • Apparently prolonged QU interval (not a true prolonged QT interval)

Although the QT interval may appear prolonged, the actual abnormality is prolongation of the QU interval due to the prominent U wave. Therefore, "prolonged QT interval" is not considered a classic ECG change of hypokalemia.

The other options are typical findings:

  • Flattening of T wave – Yes.

  • ST depression – Yes.

  • Prominent U waves – Hallmark of hypokalemia.

High-yield recall:

  • Hypokalemia: Flat T waves, ST depression, prominent U waves, prolonged QU interval.

  • Hyperkalemia: Tall peaked T waves, prolonged PR interval, widened QRS complex.

Physiology-2.question: ৮) Cardiac output increased in which of the following?
Physiology-2.exp:
Cardiac output (CO) is increased in anemia as a compensatory mechanism to maintain oxygen delivery to tissues despite reduced hemoglobin. This occurs due to:

  • Increased heart rate

  • Increased stroke volume

  • Reduced blood viscosity

  • Decreased peripheral vascular resistance

The other options are incorrect:

  • Hypothyroidism – Decreases cardiac output due to reduced metabolic rate and heart rate.

  • Hemorrhage – Decreases cardiac output because of reduced circulating blood volume.

  • Shock – Most forms (e.g., hypovolemic, cardiogenic) are associated with decreased cardiac output.

High-yield recall:

  • Cardiac output ↑: Anemia, hyperthyroidism, pregnancy, AV fistula, beriberi

  • Cardiac output ↓: Hypothyroidism, hemorrhage, cardiogenic shock, heart failure

Physiology-2.question: ৯) EDV depends on which of the following?
Physiology-2.exp:
End-diastolic volume (EDV) is the volume of blood present in the ventricle at the end of diastole. The principal determinant of EDV is venous return (preload).

Other factors also influence EDV:

  • Atrial contraction – Contributes the last 15–20% of ventricular filling.

  • Duration of diastole – Longer diastole allows more ventricular filling.

  • Distensibility (compliance) of the ventricles – More compliant ventricles can accommodate a larger EDV.

Physiology-2.question: ১০) What is the cardiac reserve in trained athlete?
Physiology-2.exp:
Cardiac reserve is the difference between the maximum cardiac output and the resting cardiac output.

Typical values:

  • Normal healthy adult: 300–400%

  • Well-trained athlete: 500–600% ✔️

  • Heart failure: May be 0% or even negative

In trained athletes:

  • Increased stroke volume

  • Enhanced myocardial contractility

  • Greater maximal cardiac output (up to 30–40 L/min)

These adaptations produce a cardiac reserve of approximately 500–600%.

High-yield recall:

  • Resting CO: ~5 L/min

  • Maximum CO (normal): ~20–25 L/min

  • Maximum CO (trained athlete): ~35–40 L/min

  • Cardiac reserve (athlete): 500–600%

Physiology-2.question: ১১) What doesn’t increases Heart Rate?
Physiology-2.exp:
Raised intracranial pressure (ICP) causes bradycardia, not tachycardia. This occurs as part of the Cushing reflex (Cushing triad):

  • Hypertension

  • Bradycardia

  • Irregular respiration

The other options all increase heart rate:

  • Temperature ✔️ – HR increases by about 10 beats/min for every 1°C rise in body temperature.

  • Adrenaline ✔️ – Stimulates β₁-adrenergic receptors, increasing heart rate.

  • Muscular exercise ✔️ – Increases sympathetic activity and decreases vagal tone, leading to tachycardia.

High-yield recall:

  • Heart rate ↑: Exercise, fever, adrenaline, hyperthyroidism

  • Heart rate ↓: Raised ICP, hypothermia, vagal stimulation

Physiology-2.question: ১২) Calculate ejection fraction if heart rate 70, cardiac output 5.6L, EDV:160ml
Physiology-2.exp:
1. Stroke Volume (SV)

SV=COHR=5600 mL/min70 beats/min=80 mLSV=HRCO​=70 beats/min5600 mL/min​=80 mL

  1. Ejection Fraction (EF)

EF=SVEDV=80160=0.5EF=EDVSV​=16080​=0.5

Answer: 0.5 (50%)

High-yield formula:

  • SV = CO ÷ HR

  • EF = SV ÷ EDV × 100%

Physiology-2.question: ১৩) What is not a features oh hypovolemic shock?
Physiology-2.exp:
Hypovolemic shock results from a significant loss of blood or body fluids, leading to decreased tissue perfusion. The body's compensatory responses include:

  • Hypotension  – Due to reduced circulating blood volume.

  • Tachycardia  – Compensatory increase in heart rate.

  • Tachypnea  – Compensatory increase in respiratory rate to improve oxygen delivery and help correct metabolic acidosis.

Bradypnea is not a feature of hypovolemic shock. It is more commonly associated with CNS depression, opioid overdose, or terminal stages of shock.

High-yield recall:

  • Hypovolemic shock: ↓BP, ↑HR, ↑RR, cold clammy skin, oliguria

  • Neurogenic shock: ↓BP + bradycardia

  • Terminal shock: May develop bradypnea

Physiology-2.question: ১৪) Which is intermediate acting BP control mechanism?
Physiology-2.exp:
Blood pressure is regulated by mechanisms based on their speed of action:

Mechanism Time of action
Baroreceptor reflex Rapid (seconds–minutes)
Chemoreceptor reflex Rapid (seconds–minutes)
CNS ischemic response Rapid (emergency response)
Capillary fluid shift mechanism Intermediate (minutes–hours) ✔️
Renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS) Long-term (hours–days)
Renal body fluid mechanism Long-term (days–weeks)

Thus, the capillary fluid shift mechanism is the intermediate-acting mechanism that restores blood volume by movement of fluid between the capillaries and interstitial space.

High-yield recall:

  • Rapid: Baroreceptors, chemoreceptors, CNS ischemic response

  • Intermediate: Capillary fluid shift, stress-relaxation, RAAS (often classified as intermediate to long-term)

  • Long-term: Renal body fluid mechanism

Physiology-2.question: ১৫) What is the change of systolic BP during sleep?
Physiology-2.exp:
During normal sleep, sympathetic activity decreases and parasympathetic tone increases, leading to:

  • Decreased heart rate

  • Decreased cardiac output

  • Reduced peripheral vascular resistance

As a result:

  • Systolic blood pressure falls by about 10–15 mmHg

  • Diastolic blood pressure also decreases slightly

This normal nocturnal fall is called "nocturnal dipping."

High-yield recall:

  • Sleep: SBP ↓ 10–15 mmHg

  • Exercise: SBP ↑, DBP unchanged or slightly ↓

  • Normal nocturnal dip: 10–20% of daytime BP

Physiology-2.question: ১৬) Which of the following regulates distribution of blood flow?
Physiology-2.exp:
Arterioles are the primary resistance vessels and are responsible for regulating the distribution of blood flow to different tissues by vasoconstriction and vasodilation.

Functions of different vessels:

  • Arteries – Conduct blood under high pressure.

  • Arterioles ✔️ – Control tissue blood flow and systemic vascular resistance.

  • Capillaries – Site of exchange of gases, nutrients, and waste products.

  • Venules – Collect blood from capillaries and begin venous return.

High-yield recall:

  • Resistance vessels: Arterioles

  • Exchange vessels: Capillaries

  • Capacitance vessels: Veins/venules

  • Conducting vessels: Arteries

Physiology-2.question: ১৭) Which is known as capacitance vessels?
Physiology-2.exp:
Veins are called capacitance vessels because they:

  • Contain 60–70% of the total blood volume at rest.

  • Have high compliance (distensibility), allowing them to store large amounts of blood with only a small increase in pressure.

  • Serve as the body's major blood reservoir.

The other options are incorrect:

  • Arteries – Conducting (pressure) vessels.

  • Arterioles – Resistance vessels.

  • Capillaries – Exchange vessels.

High-yield recall:

  • Arteries → Conducting vessels

  • Arterioles → Resistance vessels

  • Capillaries → Exchange vessels

  • Veins → Capacitance (reservoir) vessels

Physiology-2.question: ১৮) Which is a vasoconstrictor?
Physiology-2.exp:
Endothelin is one of the most potent endogenous vasoconstrictors, produced by vascular endothelial cells.

The other options are vasodilators:

  • Bradykinin – Potent vasodilator.

  • Histamine – Vasodilator; increases capillary permeability.

  • Carbon dioxide (CO₂) – Generally causes vasodilation (especially in cerebral vessels).

High-yield recall:

Vasoconstrictors:

  • Endothelin

  • Angiotensin II

  • Vasopressin (ADH)

  • Norepinephrine

Vasodilators:

  • Nitric oxide (NO)

  • Bradykinin

  • Histamine

  • Prostaglandins (PGE₂, PGI₂)

  • CO₂

Physiology-2.question: ১৯) Which of the following heart sound is produced by first rapid ventricular filling?
Physiology-2.exp:
The third heart sound (S3) is produced during the rapid ventricular filling phase of early diastole. It results from the sudden deceleration of blood entering the ventricle, causing vibration of the ventricular walls.

Heart sounds:

  • S1 – Closure of mitral and tricuspid valves (start of systole)

  • S2 – Closure of aortic and pulmonary valves (start of diastole)

  • S3 – Rapid ventricular filling (early diastole) ✔️

  • S4 – Atrial contraction against a stiff ventricle (late diastole)

High-yield recall:

  • S1: AV valve closure

  • S2: Semilunar valve closure

  • S3: Rapid ventricular filling

  • S4: Atrial systole ("atrial kick")

Physiology-2.question: ২০) What is the percentage of total blood within veins??
Physiology-2.exp:
At rest, the distribution of total blood volume is approximately:

  • Systemic veins and venules: 64% ✔️

  • Systemic arteries: 13%

  • Systemic capillaries: 7%

  • Heart: 7%

  • Pulmonary circulation: 9%

Because veins are highly compliant (capacitance vessels), they contain the largest proportion of the body's blood volume.

High-yield recall:

  • Veins & venules: 64%

  • Arteries: 13%

  • Capillaries: 7%

  • Heart: 7%

  • Pulmonary vessels: 9%

Physiology-2.question: ২১) Which of the following has highest pressure?
Physiology-2.exp:
Normal pressures of the given structures are:

  • Pulmonary artery: ≈ 25/8 mmHg (mean ≈15 mmHg) ✔️

  • Left atrium: Mean 6–12 mmHg

  • Right atrium: Mean 0–6 mmHg

  • Superior vena cava (SVC): 2–6 mmHg (similar to right atrial pressure)

Thus, among the given options, the pulmonary artery has the highest pressure.

High-yield recall:

Structure Normal pressure
Pulmonary artery 25/8 mmHg ✔️
Left atrium 6–12 mmHg
Right atrium 0–6 mmHg
SVC 2–6 mmHg

Physiology-2.question: ২২) Which electrolyte is not responsible for cardiac muscle action potential?
Physiology-2.exp:
The cardiac muscle action potential is generated by the movement of three main ions across the cell membrane:

  • Na⁺ ✔️ – Rapid depolarization (Phase 0)

  • Ca²⁺ ✔️ – Plateau phase (Phase 2) through L-type calcium channels

  • K⁺ ✔️ – Repolarization (Phase 3)

Fe²⁺ (iron) has no role in generating the cardiac action potential.

High-yield recall:

  • Phase 0: Na⁺ influx

  • Phase 1: Transient K⁺ efflux

  • Phase 2 (Plateau): Ca²⁺ influx

  • Phase 3: K⁺ efflux

  • Phase 4: Resting membrane potential (mainly K⁺ permeability)

Physiology-2.question: ২৩) Ventricular contraction causes which wave in JVP?
Physiology-2.exp:
The c wave of the jugular venous pulse (JVP) is produced during early ventricular systole when the tricuspid valve bulges into the right atrium due to ventricular contraction.

JVP waves:

  • a wave → Atrial contraction

  • c wave → Ventricular contraction causing bulging of the closed tricuspid valve ✔️

  • v wave → Venous filling of the right atrium against a closed tricuspid valve

High-yield recall:

  • a = atrial contraction

  • c = ventricular contraction (tricuspid bulging)

  • v = venous filling of right atrium

Physiology-2.question: ২৪) What is the most valuable index of ventricular function?
Physiology-2.exp:
Ejection fraction (EF) is the most valuable clinical index of ventricular (especially left ventricular) systolic function. It represents the proportion of end-diastolic blood volume ejected during systole.

EF=Stroke VolumeEnd-Diastolic Volume×100%EF=End-Diastolic VolumeStroke Volume​×100%​

Normal EF: 55–70%

The other options are less useful for assessing ventricular contractile function:

  • CO (Cardiac Output) – Influenced by heart rate and preload, not a direct measure of ventricular function.

  • EDV (End-Diastolic Volume) – Reflects preload.

  • TPR (Total Peripheral Resistance) – Reflects afterload.

High-yield recall:

  • Best index of ventricular systolic function: Ejection Fraction (EF)

  • Normal EF: 55–70%

  • Heart failure with reduced EF (HFrEF): EF < 40%

Physiology-2.question: ২৫) What is the capillary pressure (mm Hg) at venous end of capillary?
Physiology-2.exp:
The capillary hydrostatic pressure gradually falls from the arterial to the venous end:

  • Arterial end: ≈ 30–35 mmHg

  • Venous end: ≈ 10 mmHg ✔️

  • Mean capillary pressure: ≈ 17 mmHg

This pressure gradient promotes:

  • Filtration at the arterial end.

  • Reabsorption at the venous end (along with plasma oncotic pressure).

The other options are incorrect:

  • 3 mmHg – Too low (closer to central venous pressure).

  • 8 mmHg – Lower than the usual venous-end capillary pressure.

  • 30 mmHg – Characteristic of the arterial end.

High-yield recall:

  • Arterial end capillary pressure: 30–35 mmHg

  • Venous end capillary pressure: 10 mmHg

  • Plasma oncotic pressure: ≈25 mmHg

Physiology-2.question: ২৬) What is cause of QRS complex?
Physiology-2.exp:
The QRS complex on the ECG represents ventricular depolarization, which initiates ventricular systole (contraction).

  • P wave → Atrial depolarization

  • QRS complex → Ventricular depolarization → Ventricular systole ✔️

  • T wave → Ventricular repolarization

Note:
Strictly speaking, the QRS complex represents ventricular depolarization, not ventricular systole itself. However, since "ventricular depolarization" is not an option, the best answer is ventricular systole, as it immediately follows and is initiated by the QRS complex.

Physiology-2.question: ২৭) Respiratory unit includes all except ___?
Physiology-2.exp:
The respiratory unit (respiratory zone/acinus) is the part of the lung where gas exchange occurs. It includes:

  • Respiratory bronchioles

  • Alveolar ducts (often referred to as atria/antrum in some older texts)

  • Alveolar sacs

  • Alveoli

Terminal bronchioles belong to the conducting zone, not the respiratory unit, because no gas exchange occurs there.

High-yield recall:

  • Conducting zone: Trachea → Bronchi → Bronchioles → Terminal bronchioles

  • Respiratory zone (respiratory unit): Respiratory bronchioles → Alveolar ducts → Alveolar sacs → Alveoli

Note: If the option "antrum" is intended to mean alveolar atrium, then it is part of the respiratory unit. If it literally means antrum, it is an anatomically incorrect term in this context. Standard physiology MCQs expect terminal bronchioles as the exception.

Physiology-2.question: ২৮) What is the main muscle of quiet inspiration?
Physiology-2.exp:
The diaphragm is the primary muscle of quiet (normal) inspiration, contributing about 75% of the inspiratory effort. Its contraction increases the vertical diameter of the thoracic cavity, creating negative intrathoracic pressure that draws air into the lungs.

The other options:

  • External intercostals – Assist quiet inspiration by elevating the ribs but are secondary.

  • Internal intercostals – Mainly active during forced expiration (interosseous part).

  • Sternocleidomastoid – Accessory muscle of forced inspiration, not quiet breathing.

High-yield recall:

  • Quiet inspiration: Diaphragm

  • Accessory muscles (forced inspiration): Sternocleidomastoid, scalenes

  • Forced expiration: Internal intercostals, abdominal muscles

Physiology-2.question: ২৯) Lung compliance is increased in which of the following?
Physiology-2.exp:
Lung compliance is the ease with which the lungs expand.

  • Emphysema → Increased compliance due to destruction of elastic tissue and reduced elastic recoil. The lungs inflate easily but empty poorly.

  • Bronchial fibrosis → Decreased compliance.

  • Bronchiectasis → Compliance is usually normal or decreased; it is not characteristically increased.

  • Pneumonectomy → Reduces total lung volume; compliance is not increased.

High-yield recall:

  • ↑ Compliance: Emphysema, ageing

  • ↓ Compliance: Pulmonary fibrosis, pulmonary edema, ARDS, pneumonia

Mnemonic:

  • Emphysema → Easy to inflate (↑ compliance)

  • Fibrosis → Firm lungs (↓ compliance)

Physiology-2.question: ৩০) What is the percentage of cardiac output supplied to kidney?
Physiology-2.exp:
At rest, the kidneys receive approximately 20–25% of the cardiac output, which is about 1.2 L/min in a healthy adult with a cardiac output of 5–6 L/min. Among the given options, 21% is the best answer.

The kidneys receive such a large proportion of cardiac output primarily to maintain glomerular filtration, regulate fluid and electrolyte balance, and remove metabolic waste products, rather than because of high metabolic demand.

Physiology-2.question: ৩১) What is the mean pulmonary arterial pressure?
Physiology-2.exp:
The normal pulmonary arterial pressure is:

  • Systolic: ~25 mmHg

  • Diastolic: ~8 mmHg

  • Mean: ~15 mmHg ✔️

Thus, the mean pulmonary arterial pressure (mPAP) in a healthy adult at rest is 15 mmHg.

High-yield recall:

  • Pulmonary artery pressure: 25/8 mmHg

  • Mean pulmonary artery pressure (mPAP): 15 mmHg

  • Pulmonary hypertension: mPAP >20 mmHg (current definition, measured by right heart catheterization)

Physiology-2.question: ৩২) Cyanosis does not occur in ---?
Physiology-2.exp:
Cyanosis is the bluish discoloration of the skin and mucous membranes due to ≥5 g/dL of deoxygenated hemoglobin in capillary blood.

  • Polycythemia  – Cyanosis occurs readily because total hemoglobin is increased.

  • Anemia Does not usually cause cyanosis, even in hypoxemia, because the absolute amount of deoxygenated hemoglobin rarely reaches 5 g/dL.

  • Hypoxia – Can cause cyanosis if sufficient deoxygenated hemoglobin accumulates.

  • ITP – Platelet disorder; it has no direct relationship with cyanosis.

Exam point:
Although ITP does not cause cyanosis, the question asks "Cyanosis does not occur in..." as a physiology concept. The classic single best answer is anemia, because cyanosis is difficult to detect despite hypoxemia.

High-yield recall:

  • Cyanosis ↑: Polycythemia

  • Cyanosis ↓/absent: Severe anemia

  • Requires: ≥5 g/dL deoxygenated Hb

Physiology-2.question: ৩৩) Which of the following is not correct?
Physiology-2.exp:
• Anoxia – Total absence of oxygen. (Correct)

  • Dyspnea – Difficulty or labored breathing. (Correct)

  • Eupnea – Normal, quiet breathing, not cessation of breathing. (Incorrect)

  • Bradypnea – Abnormally slow breathing. (Correct)

High-yield recall:

  • Eupnea = Normal breathing

  • Apnea = Cessation of breathing

  • Dyspnea = Difficult breathing

  • Bradypnea = Slow breathing

  • Tachypnea = Rapid breathing

  • Hyperpnea = Increased depth of breathing

Physiology-2.question: ৩৪) How anatomical dead space is measured?
Physiology-2.exp:
Although Bohr's equation is primarily used to calculate physiological dead space, it is the classic exam answer for estimating anatomical dead space in physiology. Helium dilution and nitrogen washout methods measure lung volumes (especially FRC), not dead space. Fowler's method is the true method for measuring anatomical dead space, but the option is incorrectly written as "Flower's method." In most examinations, the expected answer is Bohr's equation when Fowler's method is unavailable or misspelled.

High-yield Recall:

  • Anatomical dead space: Fowler's single-breath nitrogen washout method

  • Physiological dead space: Bohr's equation

  • Helium dilution & Nitrogen washout: Measure Functional Residual Capacity (FRC), not anatomical dead space.

Physiology-2.question: ৩৫) What is the expiratory reserve volume of lung?
Physiology-2.exp:
Expiratory Reserve Volume (ERV) is the maximum additional volume of air that can be forcibly exhaled after the end of a normal tidal expiration. In a healthy adult, the average ERV is approximately 1100 mL (about 1000–1200 mL, varying with age, sex, and body build).

The other options represent different lung volumes:

  • 500 mL is approximately the Tidal Volume (TV).

  • 1200 mL is approximately the Inspiratory Reserve Volume (IRV) in some older exam keys, but the standard value of IRV is around 3000 mL in adults.

  • 3000 mL is the approximate Inspiratory Reserve Volume (IRV).

Physiology-2.question: ৩৬) what will be the type of hypoxia in CO poisoning?
Physiology-2.exp:
In carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning, CO binds to hemoglobin with approximately 200–250 times greater affinity than oxygen, forming carboxyhemoglobin (COHb). This markedly reduces the oxygen-carrying capacity of blood. In addition, CO shifts the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve to the left, impairing oxygen release to tissues.

Although the arterial PaO₂ is usually normal, the oxygen content of blood is reduced, making this a classic example of anemic hypoxia.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Hypoxic hypoxia results from low arterial oxygen tension (e.g., high altitude, severe pneumonia).

  • Stagnant hypoxia is due to reduced blood flow (e.g., heart failure, shock).

  • Histotoxic hypoxia occurs when tissues cannot utilize oxygen despite adequate delivery (e.g., cyanide poisoning).

Physiology-2.question: ৩৭) Which nerve is involved in Hering-Breuer reflex?
Physiology-2.exp:
The Hering-Breuer reflex is a protective reflex that prevents overinflation of the lungs. When the lungs are excessively inflated, pulmonary stretch receptors located in the smooth muscle of the airways are activated. The afferent impulses travel through the vagus nerve to the respiratory centers in the medulla, where inspiration is inhibited and expiration is initiated.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Glossopharyngeal nerve carries afferent fibers from the carotid body and carotid sinus, not pulmonary stretch receptors.

  • Trigeminal nerve is mainly responsible for facial sensation and muscles of mastication.

  • Facial nerve supplies the muscles of facial expression and taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.

Physiology-2.question: ৩৮) What is the location of pneumotaxic center?
Physiology-2.exp:
The pneumotaxic center is located in the upper pons, specifically in the pontine respiratory group (PRG). It regulates the pattern of breathing by limiting the duration of inspiration, thereby promoting expiration. This helps control the rate and depth of respiration. Increased activity of the pneumotaxic center produces shorter inspirations and a faster respiratory rate.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Dorsal medulla contains the dorsal respiratory group (DRG), which is primarily responsible for inspiration.

  • Anterolateral medulla contains the ventral respiratory group (VRG), involved in both inspiration and expiration, especially during forced breathing.

  • Lower pons contains the apneustic center, which promotes prolonged inspiration.

Physiology-2.question: ৩৯) Haldane effect is related to carriage of ___?
Physiology-2.exp:
The Haldane effect describes the influence of oxygenation of hemoglobin on carbon dioxide transport. When hemoglobin becomes oxygenated in the lungs, its ability to carry CO₂ and H⁺ decreases. As a result, CO₂ is released from the blood into the alveoli for exhalation.

Conversely, in peripheral tissues, deoxygenated hemoglobin has a greater capacity to bind CO₂ and H⁺, facilitating the uptake and transport of CO₂ from the tissues to the lungs.

This is different from the Bohr effect, which describes how increased CO₂ and H⁺ reduce hemoglobin's affinity for O₂, promoting oxygen release to the tissues.

Physiology-2.question: ৪০) What is the partial pressure(mmHg) of oxygen in alveolar air?
Physiology-2.exp:
The partial pressure of oxygen (PO₂) in alveolar air is approximately 104 mmHg under normal physiological conditions at sea level. Although inspired air has a PO₂ of about 159 mmHg, the alveolar PO₂ is lower because:

  • Inspired air is humidified in the respiratory tract.

  • Oxygen is continuously absorbed into the pulmonary capillary blood.

  • Carbon dioxide diffuses from the blood into the alveoli.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • 159 mmHg is the PO₂ of dry atmospheric air.

  • 149.3 mmHg is the approximate humidified inspired PO₂ after accounting for water vapor in the upper airways.

  • 120 mmHg is not a normal physiological PO₂ for alveolar air.

Physiology-2.question: ৪১) Most of the CO2 carried in the blood in the form of___?
Physiology-2.exp:
Most carbon dioxide (CO₂) is transported in the blood as bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻), accounting for approximately 70% of total CO₂ transport. Inside red blood cells, CO₂ combines with water to form carbonic acid (H₂CO₃) under the action of the enzyme carbonic anhydrase. Carbonic acid then dissociates into H⁺ and HCO₃⁻. The bicarbonate diffuses into the plasma in exchange for chloride ions, a process known as the chloride shift (Hamburger phenomenon).

The remaining CO₂ is transported:

  • About 20–23% as carbamino compounds, mainly bound to hemoglobin.

  • About 7–10% in the dissolved state in plasma.

Physiology-2.question: ৪২) Which of the following does not shift oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve to the right?
Physiology-2.exp:
A rightward shift of the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve occurs with increased H⁺ (decreased pH), increased CO₂, increased temperature, and increased 2,3-BPG. These factors decrease hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen, promoting oxygen unloading to the tissues.

In contrast, decreased H⁺ (increased pH) shifts the curve to the left, increasing hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen and enhancing oxygen loading in the lungs.

Physiology-2.question: ৪৩) The rate of gas diffusion is inversely proportional to the which of the following?
Physiology-2.option4: partial pressure difference of gas between two sides of membrane
Physiology-2.exp:
According to Fick's law of diffusion, the rate of gas diffusion across a membrane is:

  • Directly proportional to the surface area of the membrane.

  • Directly proportional to the diffusion coefficient of the gas.

  • Directly proportional to the partial pressure difference of the gas across the membrane.

  • Inversely proportional to the thickness of the membrane.

Therefore, as the thickness of the membrane increases, the rate of gas diffusion decreases. This principle explains why gas exchange is impaired in conditions such as pulmonary fibrosis and pulmonary edema, where the alveolar-capillary membrane becomes thicker.

Physiology-2.question: ৪৪) What is the normal FEV1/FVC ratio?
Physiology-2.exp:
The FEV₁/FVC ratio is the proportion of the Forced Expiratory Volume in the first second (FEV₁) to the Forced Vital Capacity (FVC). In healthy adults, the normal ratio is approximately 0.8 (80%), meaning about 80% of the vital capacity is exhaled during the first second of forced expiration.

This ratio is particularly useful in distinguishing obstructive from restrictive lung diseases:

  • In obstructive lung diseases (e.g., asthma, COPD), the FEV₁/FVC ratio decreases because FEV₁ is reduced disproportionately.

  • In restrictive lung diseases, both FEV₁ and FVC decrease proportionally, so the FEV₁/FVC ratio is usually normal or increased.

Physiology-2.question: ৪৫) which of the lung functions cannot be measured in spirometry?
Physiology-2.exp:
Spirometry measures only the volumes of air that can be inhaled or exhaled. Since Residual Volume (RV) is the amount of air that remains in the lungs after maximal forced expiration, it cannot be exhaled and therefore cannot be measured by spirometry.

In contrast:

  • Inspiratory Reserve Volume (IRV) can be measured.

  • Expiratory Reserve Volume (ERV) can be measured.

Because RV cannot be measured, lung capacities that include RV, such as Functional Residual Capacity (FRC) and Total Lung Capacity (TLC), also cannot be measured by spirometry. These require techniques such as helium dilution, nitrogen washout, or body plethysmography.

Physiology-2.question: ৪৬) What is the most abundant component of surfactant?
Physiology-2.exp:
The major and most important component of pulmonary surfactant is dipalmitoyl phosphatidylcholine (DPPC), a phospholipid produced by type II pneumocytes. DPPC is primarily responsible for reducing alveolar surface tension, thereby preventing alveolar collapse during expiration and improving lung compliance.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Proteins (surfactant proteins A, B, C, and D) constitute only a small proportion of surfactant and are involved in surfactant function and innate immunity.

  • Neutral lipids, mainly cholesterol, are present in smaller amounts and help regulate surfactant fluidity.

  • Phosphatidylglycerol is an important phospholipid but is much less abundant than DPPC.

Physiology-2.question: ৪৭) Which of the following factor does not prevent collapsing tendency of lung?
Physiology-2.exp:
The lungs have a natural tendency to collapse because of their elastic recoil and the surface tension of the alveoli. Several factors oppose this collapsing tendency:

  • Surfactant reduces alveolar surface tension, preventing alveolar collapse.

  • Negative intrapleural pressure keeps the lungs expanded by maintaining a pressure lower than atmospheric pressure within the pleural cavity.

  • Residual volume (RV) keeps some air within the lungs after maximal expiration, helping prevent complete alveolar collapse.

In contrast, positive intrapleural pressure abolishes the normal negative pleural pressure and promotes lung collapse, as occurs in pneumothorax. Therefore, it does not prevent the collapsing tendency of the lungs.

Physiology-2.question: ৪৮) How is the shape Oxyhemoglobin Ddissociation curve is __?
Physiology-2.exp:
The oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve has a sigmoid (S-shaped) configuration because of the cooperative binding of oxygen to hemoglobin. Binding of the first oxygen molecule increases the affinity of the remaining heme groups for oxygen, making subsequent oxygen binding easier. Similarly, release of one oxygen molecule facilitates the release of the others.

The plateau portion of the curve allows efficient oxygen loading in the lungs, while the steep portion promotes oxygen unloading in the tissues where it is needed most.

The other options are incorrect because the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve is not elliptical, rounded, or squared.

Physiology-2.question: ৪৯) What is called the pacemaker of heart?
Physiology-2.exp:
The sinoatrial (SA) node is the natural pacemaker of the heart because it has the highest rate of spontaneous depolarization (approximately 60–100 impulses/min). It initiates the electrical impulse that spreads through both atria and then to the AV node, coordinating normal cardiac contraction.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Purkinje fibers can generate impulses (20–40/min) but normally act only if higher pacemakers fail.

  • AV node has an intrinsic firing rate of about 40–60/min and serves as a secondary pacemaker.

  • Internodal pathways conduct impulses from the SA node to the AV node but do not generate rhythmic impulses.

Physiology-2.question: ৫০) How many leads are there in a standard ECG?
Physiology-2.exp:
A standard electrocardiogram (ECG) records the heart's electrical activity using 12 leads. These provide views of the heart from different planes and help localize cardiac abnormalities.

The 12 leads consist of:

  • 3 standard bipolar limb leads: I, II, III

  • 3 augmented unipolar limb leads: aVR, aVL, aVF

  • 6 precordial (chest) leads: V1–V6

Although only 10 electrodes are attached to the patient (4 limb electrodes and 6 chest electrodes), they generate 12 ECG leads.
